title: Elevated lipoprotein (a) and large apo(a) isoforms in Omani patients: a distinct cardiovascular risk profile

blocks.html: Elevated Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is the most common genetically inherited risk factor for cardiovascular diseases (CVD) and calcified aortic valve stenosis. Its signature protein, apolipoprotein (a) [apo(a)], contains a hypervariable number of kringle IV (KIV) domains accounting for up to 60% of Lp(a) variance [1]. Marked differences in Lp(a) concentrations and apo(a) size polymorphisms exist between ethnic groups, but data from Arab populations, who present with a higher CVD risk, remain scarce [2]. Investigating Lp(a) levels and apo(a) size polymorphism is needed to assess the specific Lp(a)-associated CVD risk, to establish adequate therapeutic thresholds, and to develop optimal clinical management strategies for populations from the Gulf region. We addressed this critical knowledge gap by measuring Lp(a) concentrations and assessing apo(a) isoform size in the Omani population.

596 Omani nationals were recruited from Muscat major hospitals including 174 healthy volunteers with no history of CVD, no cardiometabolic risk factor, no lipid-lowering treatment, and 422 patients with either familial hypercholesterolemia (FH), premature coronary artery disease (PCAD), or aortic valve stenosis (AVS). Demographic, biochemical, and clinical data (age, sex, BMI, smoking status, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and medical history of CVD) were documented. The FH subgroup included patients with either probable or definite FH according to the Dutch Lipid Clinic Network criteria. The PCAD subgroup included patients who had a first incident acute coronary event confirmed by coronary angiography before 55/65 years of age in men/women. The AVS group included patients who underwent transcatheter aortic valve implantation due to severe degenerative aortic valve stenosis. The study was approved by the research ethics committees of Sultan Qaboos University and the Ministry of Health of Oman (REF. NO. SQU-EC/386/2021, MREC #2448).

Plasma lipids were measured on a Roche COBAS C 501 analyzer. Plasma Lp(a) was measured using the apo(a) isoform-insensitive Tina-quant Lp(a) Gen. 2 immunoturbidimetric assay (Roche Diagnostics, Cat 5852641190) and categorized according to the EAS consensus statement [1]. Individual apo(a) isoform sizes were determined by Western Blot, using a validated protocol described elsewhere [3].

Statistical analyses were performed using StataNow 19.0 SE. Variables are presented as mean ± standard deviation or median and interquartile range (IQR). Comparisons between groups were made using the Kruskal–Wallis test, and correlations between variables using the Spearman’s rank test. The association between Lp(a) and CVD was assessed per 1nmol/L increase in Lp(a), and at the clinical cutoff values of 75 and 125nmol/L, using multivariable logistic regression models adjusted for sex, age, BMI, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, smoking, LDL, and HDL-cholesterol. Results are reported as odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals (OR [95% CI]). Throughout, p-values below 0.05 are considered statistically significant.

Patients more frequently suffered from coronary artery disease (48%), than from cerebrovascular disease (5%), or peripheral artery disease (1.7%). Compared with healthy volunteers, FH, PCAD, but not AVS patients, exhibited higher levels of triglycerides, total, and LDL-cholesterol but lower levels of HDL-cholesterol (Fig. 1-Panel A). Plasma Lp(a) concentrations in the patient cohort were significantly higher than those of healthy subjects, with respective median Lp(a) of 70 and 30 nmol/L (p < 0.001). Similar to LDL-cholesterol, Lp(a) plasma concentrations were maximal in the FH subgroup at 89 (28–194) nmol/L. Kernel density analysis demonstrated a markedly right-skewed distribution of Lp(a) concentrations, with patients exhibiting a broader distribution and a pronounced tail toward higher levels (Fig. 1-Panel B). Their smaller and larger apo(a) isoforms contained on average 29 (25–32) and 34 (31–36) KIV domains, respectively. As anticipated [1], there was a significant negative correlation (r = −0.262; p < 0.001) between the concentration of Lp(a) and the size of the smaller isoform but not with the size of the larger isoform (r = −0.117; p = 0.179).

sections.title: Association between Lp(a) and CVD risk

blocks.html: Given that all PCAD and AVS patients but none of the controls had suffered a cardiovascular event, we evaluated whether Lp(a) was a significant predictor of CVD only in the FH patient subgroup (n = 280). FH patients with a history of CVD had significantly higher Lp(a) concentrations compared to those without (p = 0.017) (Fig. 1-Panel C). With CVD status set as the dependent variable and Lp(a) as the explanatory variable, multivariable logistic regression analyses showed that higher Lp(a) concentrations were independently associated with increased odds of CVD. Each 1 nmol/L increase in Lp(a) levels was associated with a 0.6% increase in CVD risk (OR: 1.006, 95% CI: 1.002–1.010; p = 0.002). Likewise, FH patients with Lp(a) concentrations ≥75 nmol/L were at significantly higher risk of CVD than those with Lp(a) concentrations <75 nmol/L (OR: 3.58, 95% CI: 1.38–9.33; p = 0.009). Similarly, Lp(a) concentrations ≥125 nmol/L were strongly associated with the risk of CVD (OR: 4.54; 95% CI: 1.63–12.65; p = 0.004).

This study is the first to characterize Lp(a) levels, apo(a) isoform size, and their association with CVD in Oman. Lp(a) levels in healthy Omanis (30 nmol/L) were comparable to those of South Asians from the UK Biobank (31 nmol/L) [4]. In line with the established role of Lp(a) as a key driver of the early onset of atherosclerotic and valvular diseases [1], Lp(a) concentrations were higher in PCAD and AVS patients than in healthy controls. FH patients presented with even higher Lp(a) levels, reflecting the fact that high Lp(a) concentrations increase the likelihood for a patient to be clinically diagnosed as FH, and/or that elevated Lp(a) in FH may result from an impaired clearance of Lp(a) by the LDL receptor [5].

We uncovered that Lp(a) levels independently, significantly, and linearly increased the likelihood for a FH patient to suffer a major cardiovascular event. This highlights the additive detrimental effects of concomitantly elevated plasma Lp(a) and LDL cholesterol reported elsewhere [5], and suggests that lowering LDL cholesterol pharmacologically will not offset the specific cardiovascular risk stemming from elevated Lp(a) in FH.

To our surprise, we observed the coexistence of elevated Lp(a) plasma levels despite the expression of large apo(a) isoforms (≥23KIV domains) in a vast proportion of our patients. Unfortunately, we have not been able to determine the size of apo(a) isoforms in the healthy Omani group, which somewhat limits the scope of this observation. However, this finding contrasts with the well-established predominance of small apo(a) isoform carriers among individuals with elevated Lp(a) [1], and points toward an increased presence of genetic polymorphisms within or outside the LPA locus independent of the number of KIV repeats in this population. The presence of non-genetic factors that modulate Lp(a) production or clearance in a population-specific manner could also be at the origin of our observation. Indeed, circulating PCSK9 was found higher and correlated positively with the presence of Lp(a) particles carrying large apo(a) isoforms in African Americans but not Caucasians [6].

Our study is the first to characterize Lp(a) distribution in the Omani population. It provides key insights into the ethnic variability of Lp(a) and apo(a) isoforms in this specific population, paving the way for future research aimed at identifying Lp(a) increasing variants beyond apo(a) size polymorphism. Our observations advocate for a comprehensive assessment of Lp(a)-associated CVD risk in primary and secondary prevention Omani patients’ populations to define ethnically adequate therapeutic thresholds and optimal clinical management strategies for Oman and the Gulf region.
